hypotheses.d: Documented pressure on Assembly electors, 8 boycotts, overridden shortlist and will. The pre-arranged-pact version scores only 30% — the plan was overridden, not executed.

hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — HELD 82%
hypotheses.d: HELD. The promised authenticated footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders still has not landed, so the falsifier remains un-run. The week was IRGC-forward — the Guard, not the foreign ministry, confirmed it ran the Oman channel and announced the revenue-sharing terms, and the Guard made the mine-strike claim — but that is DENIED as a raise under the shared-prediction rule: 'the Guard runs the maritime file' is predicted just as strongly by an ordinary reading in which the IRGC is a powerful institution under a functioning Supreme Leader, which is a much weaker claim than 'the IRGC rules Iran'. The 82% cap stands for exactly the reason it was set.

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Held at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: Nobody's hurrying on Hormuz — 60% → 65% (RAISED)
hypotheses.d: Its first fact that BEATS a rival instead of merely fitting itself. On 30 Aug the US struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak after observing Guard personnel preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the strait — two days after CENTCOM declared the lanes fully cleared, and while Muscat negotiates a minesweeping calendar. The 08-30 audit had installed a genuine rival — a physical clock, minesweeping simply takes time — and ruled this hypothesis must beat it. A physical clock runs down; this one is being rewound, by the exact actor the hypothesis named in advance. Capped at +5 on three counts kept in front: CENTCOM is the interested party and 'observed preparations' is unpublished intelligence used to justify a strike; Al Jazeera published a technical challenge on 31 Aug to whether Iran can even mine by rocket as claimed; and IRGC counter-coercion against a blockade that has redirected 83 vessels, disabled three and boarded two explains the same act without any rent motive. Not pre-event.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — HELD 60%, tell sharpened
hypotheses.d: August continues the signature: 125 PLA aerial ADIZ incursions (the 2026 decline intact) against 152 non-warship PRC vessels in the first 21 days, ~60% coast guard, with the east-of-Taiwan patrols now a declared 'new normal'. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up. NOT moved — this is the same signal that bought +5 on 08-26, and re-marking on the continuation of its own evidence is the double-count the audit named. The important item is against my own test: if Beijing has DECLARED the patrols permanent, their persistence through the Sept 24 visit is close to uninformative. Re-specified now, in advance and stricter — the informative observation on 09-23→09-25 is a boarding, an inspection, or a first-time-area incursion. Mere presence no longer counts as confirmation.

hypotheses.name: Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it holds at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Falsifiers: token export volumes, Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing not actually swinging off the Middle East, or the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appearing. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Note it is DISTINCT from 'The Portfolio State' below, which is about the vehicle rather than the motive.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — HELD 52%
hypotheses.d: Confirming but shared, therefore ambience: Treasury again held back on Chinese financial institutions, with mainstream reporting now naming the mechanism outright — designating them 'could create tensions before Xi's visit'. Bessent's promised weekly cadence hit banks but no Chinese one, and at the G20 he pushed severing Iran financial ties while China dissented. Both the leverage read and the ordinary 'Washington won't detonate its own summit' read predict all of it. The strongest weekly argument AGAINST, logged rather than absorbed: the US struck Iran on three consecutive nights and took Iranian fire onto three Arab host states. Deliberate slow-walking for leverage sits badly with sustained kinetic escalation that raises the cost of the thing being slow-walked — that counterweight is what holds the number at 52.

hypotheses.name: A pre-announcement leak into oil futures — 40% → 34% (biggest mover)
hypotheses.d: Its lead conditional has now gone unfired across three weeks containing the most violently market-moving Iran news since April — the 30 Aug Larak strike, three nights of exchanges, two struck VLCCs, Brent to ~$95 — with not one reported nine-figure pre-announcement episode. The file is confirmed as historical and bounded: DOJ is probing four trades totalling ~$2.6bn, all inside a five-week window that closed in April — Mar 23 (>$500m, ~15 min before Trump's delay post), Apr 7 ($960m before the ceasefire), Apr 17 ($760m, ~20 min before Iran said Hormuz was open), Apr 21 ($430m before the extension). CORRECTION BANKED AGAINST THIS ENTRY: the ledger's earlier '~$2.2bn cluster' for Mar 23 and its '~$7bn' aggregate are both withdrawn as over-wide constructions. The cut is made on the hypothesis's own written terms, not on a preferred reading — a conditional set at 60% has burned three of fourteen weeks in the best environment it will ever get and produced nothing. The cut is only −6 because of one genuinely new structural fact: investigators are running a SEPARATE probe into prediction-market activity on the same developments, and the same foreknowledge reaching two unrelated venues is hard to explain as one market-maker hedging client flow. Split now: deliberate leak 34 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 36 / coincidence 10. Still the only entry whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event.

hypotheses.name: NEW · The Portfolio State — coercion converted into sovereign equity, statute retrofitted
hypotheses.d: Strongest form: the US is converting military and sanctions leverage into permanent state equity in strategic supply chains, with the legal authority written to fit transactions rather than the reverse — Venezuela being the first hydrocarbon use of a template already run in chips and critical minerals. The rail predates the headline, which is the only thing licensing a design read at all: Senate NDAA FY2027 §1051 was marked up in MID-JUNE — ten weeks before the 29 Aug deal — creating a DoD Equity Investment Account, authorising OSC equity to $500m and capping any single position at 40% of the entity; the Venezuela stake is 35%, inside a cap that does not legally exist yet. Add DoD's own $400m/15% stake in MP Materials with 100% offtake (structurally identical to Venezuela's '20% of output at cost'), House Oversight already demanding an accounting of Venezuelan oil revenue on 23 Feb, and CFR's tally of 26 government equity deals worth ~$23.9bn. It opens at only 25% because the boring, incompetence and patronage readings are all strong: think tanks have been publicly naming and counting this pattern since 2025 (a policy, not a plot); the Pentagon's own spokesman flatly DENIES that OSC takes equity while WSJ reports it doing so, which is improvisation not design; and a 100-year concession over 65bn bbl routed to one politically connected operator with no published contract is better explained as spoils allocation. Above all the base rate is enormous — Anglo-Persian 1914, the RFC, GM/Chrysler 2009 — so the design premium must be small. NOT a conspiracy claim and must never be scored as one: it requires no secrecy at all, only anticipation, and the honest gap is that I cannot name the operator who executes the warrants. Key test: does the ENACTED NDAA widen §1051 beyond critical minerals to energy, or raise the cap, by 31 Dec (45%)? Scope enacted unchanged kills the design read.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 25% → 22% (CUT, sixth session running)
hypotheses.d: The week finally produced Russia-Iran material and it is the wrong KIND. Moscow said publicly on 01 Sep that air defence is the main focus of military-technical cooperation with Iran, alongside a reported 500 Verba MANPADS and 2,500 missiles and continued fighter deliveries. That is the resupply leg — already priced at 7/10 under 'means'. It moves nothing: it is announced by TASS, an interested party publishing its own helpfulness and the structural opposite of a covert channel; the opportunism branch predicts arms sales to a client at war identically, so under the standing rule it is ambience; and after six sessions there is still ZERO documentary evidence Moscow has influenced Tehran's negotiating position, which is the actual claim. Arms transfers are not persuasion. Cut rather than held because a decay rule that bites only on its deadline is a cliff, not decay. Clock unchanged: 15% on 30 Sep absent documentary evidence, retire below 10%.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Nothing resolved this week, and one file addition cuts against it: the summit's Iran content is now openly reported as an explicit US ask — Chinese pressure on Tehran to reopen the strait — with Beijing expected to want Taiwan concessions in return. An openly negotiated Iran-for-Taiwan trade is this hypothesis's RIVAL, not its confirmation; the secret-package version needs the deal hidden, and the deal is being conducted in headlines. Retirement trigger unchanged; the test runs on schedule on 24 Sept.

brief.head: Israel shuts Britain's Jerusalem consulate over settlement ban
brief.h: Hours after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament that Israeli settlers were carrying out "ethnic cleansing" in the West Bank and announced a ban on goods and some services from the settlements, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar ordered Britain's consulate in east Jerusalem closed, expelled British diplomats from the centre monitoring the US-brokered Gaza ceasefire, barred British training of Palestinian Authority forces and banned 12 British officials from entering Israel.
brief.t: The load-bearing distinction is speed. Britain's ban is an announcement that officials say will take six to nine months to bite and may need primary legislation rather than a statutory instrument; Israel's answer was effective on Tuesday. So London traded a future, revocable instrument for an immediate and concrete loss of presence - a consulate in east Jerusalem that handles Palestinian consular business, a seat in the Gaza ceasefire monitoring centre, and a training relationship with the Palestinian Authority's security forces. Follow the money and the trade turns out not to be the point: total UK-Israel goods and services trade was about GBP 6bn in 2025 and settlement output is a rounding error inside it. What is actually being spent is access. And note the clock Saar named out loud - Israel votes on 27 October with Netanyahu campaigning on the settlements, which makes a foreign attack on them a campaign asset rather than a cost.
brief.context: The legal rail predates the headline: the ICJ's July 2024 advisory opinion on the unlawfulness of the occupation gave European governments a text to cite, and Britain had already suspended free-trade talks and sanctioned individual settlers in May 2025. Tuesday extends that from persons to commerce, and France and Canada moved with it in a joint statement. The desk that decides is not the Foreign Office podium but the Department for Business and Trade drafting the instrument and the whips finding parliamentary time, because a goods ban that needs primary legislation is a queue, not a decision. Base rate: the EU's 2015 settlement labelling rules and the 2019 ECJ ruling made settlement goods identifiable across a market twenty times the size of Britain's, and settlement construction did not measurably slow - which is the honest prior for how much a trade measure moves facts on the ground. What would change that read is the services half, which is new: financing, construction, infrastructure, real estate and advertising are where settlement expansion is actually capitalised, and no previous European measure touched them.

angles.effect: gains - a moral position that costs almost nothing in trade, delivered to a domestic coalition that has demanded it for a year

angles.party: Netanyahu's campaign, 49 days from the 27 October vote
angles.effect: gains - a foreign government attacking the settlements is free advertising for a platform built on them

angles.party: British diplomacy in Jerusalem and Gaza
angles.effect: pays - the consulate closes and British monitors leave the ceasefire centre, immediately and unilaterally
pay - British training ends, which removes a capability without touching a settler

dec.kill: A statutory instrument or bill laid before Parliament with a commencement date. If nothing is tabled within three months, the announcement was a statement of intent and Israel's counter-move was the only binding thing that happened on Tuesday.

consp.claim: That the settlement ban is a decoy timed to bury domestic stories about policing and immigration, and that Washington and Jerusalem will now punish Britain for it - with the consulate closure read as the first instalment and the US-UK trade relationship named as the next target.
consp.spread: Two Brit/pol/ generals running at 280 and 129 replies through Tuesday and a thread headed "Israel and America THREATEN Britain!" at 145 replies. A separate strand inside the same threads carries an ethnic-scapegoat narrative about who is said to direct British foreign policy; the technique is substituting an ethnic "who" for the coalition question of which lobbies raise the price of defection.
consp.read: The decoy half is the standard dead-cat frame and is not checkable in either direction. The retaliation half is not a theory at all - Saar announced it on the record within hours - so the board is narrating something that had already happened and experiencing it as prophecy, which is how a frame earns credibility it never paid for. The kernel actually worth watching is the American one: whether Washington attaches any cost to the British move, or lets it pass.

brief.head: Iran says it captured an American robot submarine in Hormuz
brief.h: The IRGC Navy said it intercepted and seized an advanced unmanned American underwater vehicle at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Tuesday after a "complex intelligence and operational action"; Tasnim identified it as an Anduril Dive-LD - 5.8 metres, 2.7 tonnes, ten days' endurance, delivered to the US Navy's Unmanned Undersea Vehicle Group 1 in 2025 - and Naval News, examining the released photograph, found the flood holes, fastenings and small forward mast match that model.
brief.t: Separate the two claims, because only one of them is corroborated. That the object is a Dive-LD is now supported by an independent imagery desk reading the same photograph. How it came to be in Iranian hands is not: a vehicle recovered adrift or aground looks identical in a still image to a vehicle ambushed, and the phrase "complex intelligence and operational action" is doing unpaid work. The reason this does not move the escalation gate is structural, and it is the whole point of unmanned systems - an American asset was taken and there is no American body. Ownership without casualty is the cheapest possible loss. The prize is also not the hull; it is the autonomy stack and whatever the recorder held, which is why the consequential question here is not Iranian but Russian and Chinese.
brief.context: R0 dates this to the unmanned-attrition rail rather than to the war: the state that can afford to lose robots wins the presence contest, and the state that captures one gets a technology transfer it did not fund. The physical board matters more than the rhetoric - the strait has been shut to commercial traffic for 192 days by war-risk pricing rather than by mines, with IMF PortWatch counting six transits on 30 August against a typical 85 a day, war-risk premiums running at roughly 40 times pre-crisis and six P&I clubs having withdrawn cover. Against that, one drone changes no premium. The desk that decides is not CENTCOM's podium but Anduril's classification authority and the Navy's damage assessment. Base rate: Iran has taken American unmanned systems before - the RQ-170 in 2011, two Saildrones seized and returned within a day in 2022 - and the American response was procedural every time. Falsifier, dated: if Washington confirms a loss and responds kinetically within thirty days, the "robots are the deniability layer" read is wrong and this board must say so.

angles.effect: gains - a photographable win in a month when a US tanker-for-tanker campaign has been disabling its hulls
pay - an autonomy stack in hostile hands, and a loss they have neither confirmed nor denied
gain if the hull is shared - counter-UUV work they did not have to pay for
pays nothing today - the strait was already closed by insurance, so this moves no premium

dec.kill: A US Navy statement confirming or denying the loss, and whether Iranian state television shows the vehicle intact with its payload bay open. If the release stays a single still photograph, treat the "complex operational action" framing as decoration on the recovery of something adrift.

consp.claim: That Iran will now reverse-engineer the vehicle into cheap mass-produced "underwater Shaheds" - and, in a louder parallel thread, that Iran has begun sinking American supercarriers while Trump quietly withdraws.
consp.spread: A dedicated capture thread on /pol/, a 125-reply thread celebrating the seizure, and a 65-reply thread headed "TRUMP WITHDRAWING AS IRAN BEGINS SINKING US SUPER CARRIERS"; the Persia-Israel general at 316 replies carries "Iran is shooting anti-ship cruise missiles on USN" in its item list.
consp.read: The underwater-Shahed claim is the strongest version and is an industrial argument rather than a fantasy - Iran attempted exactly this with the RQ-170 airframe after 2011, though the copy took years and never matched the original's sensors, and a 6,000-metre-rated autonomous hull is a harder problem than a subsonic airframe. The carrier claim has no wire, no imagery and no missing hull, and belongs to the standing family in which a decisive blow has already landed and is being suppressed. The tell is that the same thread set reads an American withdrawal and an American escalation as equally confirming.

brief.head: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats in a break with Orban's line
brief.h: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orban ordered ten Russian diplomats out of Hungary on Tuesday for activities "incompatible with their diplomatic status", saying the decision protects "Hungary's security and sovereignty" and does not mean breaking off relations with Moscow; Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova promised a "harsh and painful" response, and Commission spokesman Christian Wigand called it a legitimate decision.
brief.t: This is what an election result looks like when it finally reaches the plumbing. Hungary was the one EU member state that did not join the expulsion wave after 2022, and it is joining now - four and a half months after Viktor Orban lost power following sixteen years in office. The Kremlin's Central European veto player was never a country; it was a governing coalition, and the coalition is gone. Read the construction rather than the rhetoric: ten officers, an explicit statement that relations are not being severed, and a legal formula that requires no evidence to be published. That is a state testing how much it can charge Moscow without triggering the answer that would actually hurt, which is not a diplomatic one.
brief.context: The rail is physical, not sentimental. Hungary's exposure to Russia is TurkStream pipeline gas and the Rosatom-built Paks nuclear complex, whose expansion Moscow both finances and constructs - which is why a new government that wants to demonstrate realignment does it with accreditations rather than with contracts. The desk that decides is therefore not the foreign ministry but MVM, the state energy company, and whoever holds the winter supply schedule. Base rate: European expulsion rounds since the 2018 Skripal wave have produced mirrored expulsions and essentially no interruption to commercial energy flow, and Moscow's "harsh and painful" formula has historically resolved into a matching number of Hungarian diplomats sent home. The second-order effect is the one Brussels cares about: unanimity votes on Russia sanctions had a reliable holdout, and this is the clearest signal yet that they no longer do. What would change the read is any interruption to TurkStream deliveries or a Rosatom slowdown at Paks - that would mean Moscow decided to make an example of a defector rather than absorb the loss.

angles.effect: gains - cheap, legible proof to Brussels that the Orban era is over, at the price of ten accreditations
pays - its last friendly intelligence platform sited inside the EU's decision-making rooms
gains - a unanimity problem on Russia sanctions it may no longer have to route around
carry the risk - the exposure is TurkStream and Paks, and any bill for this arrives in winter, not this week

dec.kill: TurkStream volumes into Hungary and the Paks II construction schedule. If both run unchanged through the heating season, "harsh and painful" meant ten Hungarian diplomats expelled from Moscow and nothing else.

brief.head: Russian drone hits Kyiv TV newsroom hours before Trump calls Putin
brief.h: A Russian drone struck the Kyiv headquarters of the channel We Are Ukraine while journalists were broadcasting live, partially collapsing the building; five people were killed in Kyiv across the overnight and daytime strikes with 25 wounded, a rail employee was killed in an attack on a passenger train in the south, and on Tuesday evening Putin's senior adviser Yuriy Ushakov said the two presidents had spoken for an hour in a "constructive and very frank" call, on which the White House has said nothing.
brief.t: Read the sourcing before the sentiment. Every adjective attached to that call comes from the Kremlin; the American side has published nothing, and Steve Witkoff's only comment after the Moscow and Kyiv shuttle was that "substantive progress" had been made, with no detail behind it. When one party narrates a negotiation alone, the narration is the product. Now set it against what Moscow did in daylight the same day - a drone into a live newsroom, which the channel says its own footage shows was deliberate. The pairing is the analysis: for Russia, talking and striking are not alternatives to be traded off, they are the same instrument, and demonstrating that is itself a negotiating position.
brief.context: The rail is the 72-hour capitals pause that expired on Monday. Quiet was granted for the duration of a visit and withdrawn at its end, which established that Moscow owns the switch - and a party that owns the switch has no reason to sell it cheaply. The desk that decides is not the podium but the Russian long-range aviation tasking cycle and Ushakov's readout discipline, which has been consistent for a year: Moscow publishes first, warmly, and without commitments. Base rate: there have been several hour-long Trump-Putin calls since 2025 and none has been followed within a month by a verified fall in strike tempo. BBC Verify now measures Kyiv air-raid alerts at their highest level since the 2022 invasion, which is the opposite of the trace a de-escalating negotiation leaves. Zelensky, after meeting Witkoff and Kushner in Kyiv on Sunday - their first visit - said he expects the war to run into winter and asked for a trilateral. What would change the read: an American readout naming a concession by either side, or a dated pause that is not tied to a visit.

angles.effect: gains - it wrote the only account of the call, so "constructive and very frank" enters the record unopposed
gains - a live channel to Moscow with no published commitments and therefore nothing to defend
pay - a newsroom hit on air, and a signal about which civilian categories now sit inside the target set
pays - talks proceed while the strike tempo sits at a record, which prices Kyiv's time as the cheap commodity in the room

dec.kill: A White House or State Department readout of the call. If Washington never publishes one, the only account of what the American president agreed to remains a Russian account - and that absence is itself the finding.

consp.claim: That Ukraine has already lost and the Witkoff-Kushner shuttle was a surrender negotiation dressed as diplomacy - with a companion strand holding that Ukraine's own services, the SBU and HUR, have been shooting at each other on the streets of Kyiv, and that Russia is seizing private companies by designating them "extremist organisations".
consp.spread: A 128-reply thread built on Owen Matthews's Spectator piece of 7 September arguing Ukraine is losing, plus the Ukraine happening general at 212 replies carrying the SBU-versus-HUR item and the company-seizure item in its header list.
consp.read: Unusual for this section in that the core claim is not fringe - it is a named columnist in a mainstream magazine, and the boards are amplifying an argument rather than inventing one. The checkable kernel is the SBU-HUR item, which traces to a real Zelensky remark calling an armed confrontation between the services a disgrace and has been stretched into a civil-war reading. What all of it is downstream of is the missing American readout: when only one side narrates, the vacuum fills with the most dramatic story on offer.

brief.head: US ends the licence that let Iranian-Americans send money home
brief.h: The wind-down window under OFAC General License BB closed on Tuesday, and with it the standing authorisations for non-commercial personal remittances to Iran, academic and educational exchanges, conference-related services and sports exchanges that Treasury suspended on 24 August under "Operation Economic Outcast"; anyone continuing those activities now needs a specific licence applied for case by case, and Reuters reported fresh Iran-related designations posted to the Treasury website the same day.
brief.t: The whole story sits in the difference between two words. A general licence is a standing permission a bank compliance desk can rely on without asking anyone; a specific licence is an application, a queue, a legal opinion and a file. Convert that into behaviour and the paperwork stops mattering: no correspondent bank will process a five-hundred-dollar transfer to a grandmother in Isfahan while the authorisation is a pending application, so the effective policy is a stop regardless of what the regulation formally says. Then follow who pays. The Iranian state does not move money through non-commercial personal remittance channels - it funds itself through crude, front companies and the Turkish banking corridor Treasury designated four days earlier. Iranian-American families, university exchange offices and sports federations do. Name the mechanism: general-licence withdrawal is the cheapest coercive instrument in the toolkit, because Treasury never has to enforce it. The banks enforce it for free, by de-risking.
brief.context: The rail is older than the war. Non-commercial personal remittances have been authorised under the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations for years precisely because Washington's stated position is that its quarrel is with the Iranian government and not the Iranian people; suspending the authorisation retires that distinction without ever announcing that it has been retired, which is why the caveat matters more than the headline. The desk that decides is OFAC's licensing division and, far more decisively, the compliance departments at the handful of institutions still willing to touch Iran-adjacent flows. Base rate: when a general licence is replaced by a specific-licence requirement, the observed outcome is near-total cessation of the activity rather than a slower version of it, because the application cost exceeds the value of an individual transaction by orders of magnitude - the same dynamic that emptied humanitarian channels to Afghanistan and Syria after 2021. What would change the read: a published humanitarian carve-out, a fast-track, or a granted specific licence for remittances becoming public.

angles.effect: gains - a headline metric of escalation that requires no enforcement action, no seizure and no litigation risk
pay - the one channel in the programme that touches households rather than the state

angles.party: US universities, conference organisers and sports federations
angles.effect: pay - exchange arrangements that now need case-by-case licences with no published timetable
largely unaffected on this instrument - it is funded by oil and front companies, not by relatives wiring money home

dec.kill: A published OFAC humanitarian carve-out or a granted specific licence covering personal remittances. If one appears within a month, this was a pressure signal with a release valve; if the queue simply stays silent, the general licence was the policy all along and its removal is the policy now.

consp.claim: That the sanctions programme is "Economic D-Day" - a campaign to collapse the Iranian economy outright rather than to change its behaviour - circulating alongside a heavily reposted presidential claim that oil will fall to three dollars a gallon and ultimately below two once the war is won.
consp.spread: The Persia-Israel general on /pol/ has been counting "Day 18 of Economic D-Day" in its header at 316 replies, and a separate thread reposting the two-dollars-a-gallon line drew mockery at 21 replies against a live Brent price near $98.
consp.read: The "D-Day" label is the boards' own name for a real and dated thing - Operation Economic Outcast was announced on 24 August and the wind-down expired on Tuesday - so the kernel is simply true and the only disagreement is about intent, which is not observable and therefore not scoreable. The two-dollar claim is the checkable half and the tape currently falsifies it; watch for the standard repair, which is a quiet restatement with a longer horizon rather than a withdrawal.

watch: A statutory instrument or bill laid before Parliament on the settlement trade ban, with a commencement date. This is the kill criterion on the lead card: officials briefed six to nine months and hinted that a goods ban may need primary legislation rather than a statutory instrument. If nothing is tabled within three months, the only binding thing that happened on Tuesday was Israel closing the consulate.

Brent's CLOSE, every day to 24 September. The board's oldest scoreable question resolves on closes, not intraday prints, and Tuesday delivered exactly the illustration - a $99.09 high and a ~$97.40 late print off the same event. This is the observable that produces this board's first Brier score in 31 open questions.

A US Navy statement on the Dive-LD, and whether Iranian state television shows the vehicle intact with its payload bay open. The identification is corroborated; the capture story is not. A single still photograph and nothing further would point to a recovery being dressed as an operation - and the second-order question is onward transfer to Russia or China.

TurkStream volumes into Hungary and the Paks II construction schedule. Zakharova's harsh and painful formula has historically resolved into a mirrored expulsion and nothing else. If gas or the Rosatom build slips this heating season, Moscow decided to make an example of a defector, which is a different and much larger story.

A White House or State Department readout of Tuesday's hour-long call. As of Tuesday night the only account of what the American president discussed with Putin is Yuriy Ushakov's. If Washington never publishes one, that silence is the finding and it prices Kyiv's negotiating position for the rest of the month.
lesson: Today's lesson is about proxies, and it explains why this board refused to raise its Iran forecast on a day when Iranian-aligned forces set Saudi oil sites on fire. When a state fights through someone else's army, it is buying a specific product: deniability. Idean Salehyan's work on the delegation of war to non-state groups sets out the trade - the sponsor gets cheapness and a plausible shrug, and pays for it with a principal-agent problem, because the proxy has its own war aims and can drag the sponsor somewhere it did not choose to go. Thomas Schelling's companion idea is that the ambiguity is not a bug: an attack nobody can cleanly attribute is a threat that is hard to answer without escalating first, which is why the wrapper is worth paying for. The base rate is where this stops being theory. On 14 September 2019, drones and cruise missiles knocked 5.7 million barrels a day - half of Saudi output - out of Abqaiq and Khurais; the Houthis claimed it, Washington publicly blamed Iran, UN monitors later found the Houthis could not have done it, and the American response was a troop deployment and sanctions, not a strike on Iran. So here is the discipline the lesson yields, and it is testable: attribution is not a trigger, ownership is. Watch whether anything hits an ASSET the United States must answer for - a US-flagged hull, an American casualty - because that, not the size of the fire in Jazan, is the variable that has historically moved American decisions.

events.label: Abha / Khamis Mushait
events.note: Houthi drones and ballistic missiles struck a coalition airbase at Khamis Mushait and Aramco sites at Abha, part of a four-city wave that wounded 73 including women and children and halted operations at some energy facilities. Both towns sit close to the Yemeni border, well inside Houthi range - which is why the 2019 range objection does not transfer here.

quiz.q: Iranian-aligned forces set fire to Saudi oil facilities, and this board did NOT raise its forecast of a renewed US or Israeli strike campaign on Iran. What is the stated reason?
options: Because the attack was too small to matter to oil markets
Because in 2019 a far larger attack on Saudi oil - Abqaiq, half the kingdom's output - produced no American strike on Iran
Because the Houthis are not connected to Iran in any way
Because the US has publicly ruled out further strikes on Iran
quiz.why: The base rate is the discipline. Abqaiq removed 5.7 million barrels a day, was blamed on Iran by Washington, and produced a troop deployment and sanctions - not a strike. Damage to Saudi assets has historically not been the trigger; damage to American ones has, which is why this board's CRITICAL gate is a struck US-flagged hull or an American death rather than a burning refinery.

quiz.q: The brief says the Jazan complex is the asset that converts a Yemeni grievance into a global price. Why Jazan specifically rather than the size of any fire?
options: Because Jazan is where most Saudi crude is loaded for export
Because it is a 400,000 b/d refinery, about a tenth of Aramco's net refining capacity, and the world is short conversion capacity rather than crude
Because it is the closest facility to Iran
Because Jazan produces most of Saudi Arabia's electricity
quiz.why: A barrel of crude is not a usable product. The binding constraint in this cycle is the capacity to turn crude into diesel, so hitting a refinery bites harder per unit of damage than hitting a wellhead. Crude exports load at Ras Tanura and Yanbu, hundreds of miles from anything struck on Tuesday - which is why the brief's kill criterion is loadings, not fires.

quiz.q: Russia paused strikes on Kyiv for exactly the 72 hours that US envoys were in the region, then fired 166 drones. What does the brief say that timing reveals?
options: That Russia is running out of missiles and needed to reload
That Moscow can switch the air campaign on and off at will, which indicates confidence rather than exhaustion
That the pause was imposed on Russia by the United States
That Ukraine's air defences were down during the visit
quiz.why: A truce whose duration matches an itinerary to the hour is a scheduling accommodation, not a de-escalation - and the precision is itself the information. Fortna's finding is that ceasefires without monitors, guarantors or a demilitarised separation fail at high rates, and this arrangement had none of the three, which is why the 30-day ceasefire forecast was cut rather than raised.

quiz.q: The brief argues that stablecoins and the Fed's bill programme cannot fix Britain's 5.89 per cent thirty-year yield. What is the mechanism?
options: Because those programmes create demand for SHORT paper - bills - so the bid concentrates at the front of the curve and the long end is left to private buyers
Because the Bank of England is prohibited from buying gilts
Because stablecoins are illegal in the United Kingdom
Because thirty-year debt is not sold at auction
quiz.why: Tokenised dollar claims have to be backed by something short and liquid, which means Treasury bills. That manufactures a bid at the front end and does nothing for thirty-year duration, which is left to pension funds, insurers and price-sensitive foreigners who charge for inflation risk. Hence the brief's line that the long end is the leg no monetary innovation repairs.

quiz.q: CRITICAL THINKING. A widely circulated report puts transshipment - Chinese goods relabelled through third countries - at up to $303bn. Which observable best tests that CLAIM?
options: Whether the total Chinese trade surplus keeps rising
Whether more governments publicly endorse the report
Whether the rerouting rate holds up when customs data are matched WITHIN individual firms rather than at the product level
Whether Vietnam's exports to the US grew faster than its exports elsewhere
quiz.why: The size of the number depends almost entirely on how coarsely you match the data. Academic work found about 16.5 per cent of US-bound Vietnamese exports looked rerouted at the national product level, 6.5 per cent within provinces, and 1.7 per cent within individual firms - meaning aggregation was mistaking one company's genuine production for another's rerouting. The claim is checkable, and the check is firm-level matching.

sections.t: US diesel set an all-time record this week at $5.820 a gallon, and the crack spread — the refiner's fee for turning crude into something an engine can burn — printed an all-time $108 a barrel while Brent sat at an unremarkable $96. In the same week US missiles reportedly struck a tanker at Iran's Kharg Island anchorage, and Ukrainian drones held Russian refinery runs at 3.6m barrels a day, the lowest since May 2002.

Crude — the thing everyone photographs and embargoes — is behaving; refined product is not. A $108 crack means the market will pay more to convert a barrel than the barrel is worth: a fact about cokers and hydrotreaters, not about oil. Name the mechanism — the conversion bottleneck. The binding constraint is never the abundant input but the narrow step in the middle, which cannot be built on the timescale of a war or an election.

sections.h: Deep history I — Rockefeller never wanted the oil
sections.t: John D. Rockefeller owned almost no wells. He owned the refineries of Cleveland, and what he did with them in 1871 is the founding text of chokepoint economics. Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad chartered the South Improvement Company, and Rockefeller's terms inside it were breathtaking: the Erie, New York Central and Pennsylvania would pay the SIC a rebate of $1.06 on every barrel it shipped — and a drawback of $1.06 on every barrel shipped by refiners outside the club. He was paid when his rivals did business. The charter was repealed that April before a single transaction cleared, and Ida Tarbell's exposé later finished the job — but the insight outlived the scandal: crude is worthless until someone converts and moves it, and whoever owns the narrow step prices the wide one.

sections.h: Deep history II — the war decided at the still
sections.t: The largest test of this proposition was the Allied air war, fought inside the alliance before it was fought over Germany. Arthur Harris of RAF Bomber Command believed in punishment: burn the cities, break the will. Carl Spaatz and Arthur Tedder pushed what Harris dismissed as panacea targets — oil. Germany had almost no crude. It had Bergius hydrogenation, synthetic fuel pressed from coal at Leuna, Pölitz and Brüx, plants too enormous to hide. The oil plan began in May 1944. Leuna alone absorbed 22 raids, 6,552 bomber sorties and 18,328 tons of bombs across a year, behind Europe's heaviest flak concentration. It worked anyway. German synthetic output fell from a peak of 316,000 tons a month to 107,000 in June 1944 and 17,000 by September. Aviation gasoline — the specific fraction, not oil in general — went from 175,000 tons in April to 5,000 in September: 97% gone in five months. From May 1944 Germany consumed more than it produced every month, and the stockpile was gone in six.

sections.h: Deep history II — the fuel, not the factories
sections.t: The detail that makes it unforgettable: over the same period Albert Speer drove German tank and aircraft PRODUCTION to its wartime peak. The Reich ended 1944 with more airframes than it could fly and more panzers than it could move — the factories were fine and the fuel was not. The US Strategic Bombing Survey — written by people with every reason to praise bombing in general — judged the oil and transport campaigns decisive and the city campaign not. Japan lost the same way: the July 1941 freeze is remembered as an oil embargo, but the fatal shortage was 100-octane aviation gasoline, a conversion capability Japan could not build.

sections.h: Deep history III — how the West stopped building stills
sections.t: Now the slow part. The last greenfield major refinery built in the United States was Marathon's Garyville, Louisiana: built 1973-76, online 1977, still running at 596,000 barrels a day. Fifty years, no new plants — and the base is now shrinking: about 132 operable refineries in January 2025 against more than 300 in 1981, with roughly 1.235m b/d of distillation capacity removed in seven recent closures and conversions, over 6.5% of the total. All of it while shale made America the largest crude producer in history at 13.86m b/d. The country built the well and stopped building the still. The capacity emigrated rather than vanished — Jamnagar runs 1.24m b/d, Dangote opened at 650,000 and plans 1.4m, China kept building — so the toll moved east and south, to jurisdictions happy to buy discounted sanctioned crude and sell the product back to the people imposing the sanctions.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: In all three cases the scarce thing is the transformation, and transformation capacity is inelastic over any politically relevant horizon: a new crude supplier takes a fortnight, a new hydrocracker takes five years and a billion dollars. Ukraine is now running the 1944 oil plan at a ten-thousandth of the cost, a drone flying 1,550km to Omsk doing what 6,552 B-17 sorties did to Leuna — Pape's denial thesis tested live. It breaks against me here: Germany had no crude and no neutral supplier, Russia has both, and a 24-year low in refining has not stopped Pokrovsk.

sections.h: The adjudication — Yergin and Blas vs Chris Miller
sections.t: THE ADJUDICATION — YERGIN AND BLAS versus CHRIS MILLER Yergin and Blas hold that energy chokepoints self-heal — inventories, bypass and rerouting absorb shocks forecast to be fatal — and they have been right about the barrel, Brent at $96 in a war that curtailed over 11m b/d. Chris Miller's Chip War argues the opposite for inputs that are not fungible: no reserve of fabs, no bypass for EUV, a decade to rebuild. The evidence splits them by step. Yergin and Blas won the crude argument; the crack is the market announcing the win does not survive one step downstream, because there is no strategic reserve of cokers — the US holds hundreds of millions of barrels of crude in the SPR and about a million barrels of distillate in the Northeast reserve, having stockpiled the input it cannot burn. Miller's case is still weaker in oil than in silicon: diesel is shippable in a way a fab's output is not, so refining heals in 12-24 months rather than 12-24 days.

OECD gasoline demand is in structural decline as EVs scale; diesel and jet demand are not, because trucks, ships, aircraft, mining and data-centre backup have no substitute. But a refinery makes every cut at once, so the economics that close Western refineries — falling gasoline — destroy the distillate capacity nobody meant to lose. A trap, not a cycle; confidence high. The bolder call, near 60%: by the mid-2030s the US is at once the world's largest crude exporter and a chronic net importer of middle distillates, and that buys a strategic PRODUCT reserve — legislated storage of diesel and jet, enacted after a winter shortage rather than before one. What keeps this honest is GEO-026: does the US diesel crack settle below $45 before 15 December 2026? It sits at 35%, so the house is 65% on regime rather than outage — and if the crack mean-reverts on the 2022 schedule, this is an elegant story about a spike, published as a miss.
